# Incident Report — Network Traffic Analysis
**Evidence:** `2024-08-15-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (18,189 packets, 2024-08-15 04:09:43–04:42:26, capture clock UTC+4). No IDS/Suricata export was present in the evidence folder; findings are derived entirely from packet-level analysis with `tshark`.

## Victim host
| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.8.15.133** |
| MAC address | **00:1c:bf:03:54:82** (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-H8ALZBV** |
| AD domain | LAFONTAINEBLEU.ORG (NetBIOS `LAFONTAINEBLEU`, DC `WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS.lafontainebleu.org` at 10.8.15.4) |
| Logged-in user | **plucero** (confirmed via Kerberos AS-REQ, `CNameString: plucero`, realm `LAFONTAINEBLEU.ORG`) |

Confirmed by cross-referencing DHCP (hostname option), NBNS, ARP, and Kerberos traffic — all point to the same IP/MAC/hostname.

## Infection chain (reconstructed from traffic)
1. **04:11:15** — `10.8.15.133` sent a Chrome/Edge-127 browser GET to `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (104.21.55.70, Cloudflare-fronted) with a tracking query string. The server immediately returned a **200 OK** with `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="Invoice 876597035_003.zip"` — a fake-invoice/phishing lure delivering a file directly on first request.
   - Zip SHA256: `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5`
   - Contains a single file: **`Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js`** (6,990,020 bytes), SHA256: `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c`
   - The JS is bulked out with ~7MB of scraped filler text (technical-standard/report excerpts) used purely as padding/anti-AV bloat; it contains a hardcoded `WScript.Sleep(10000)` (sandbox-evasion delay) and a callback URL to `https://business.checkfedexexp.com/data-privacy?...` (confirmed resolved via DNS later in the capture).
2. **04:12:00** — The host used **Microsoft BITS/7.8** (bitsadmin) to fetch a file from a raw IP with no preceding DNS lookup: `HEAD`/`GET http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4`. Abusing BITS to fetch a payload (rather than the malware's own process) is a known LOLBin technique (MITRE T1197) that blends the download in with legitimate Windows Update BITS jobs seen elsewhere in this same capture.
   - Downloaded file is a **PE32+ DLL**, 159,232 bytes, SHA256: **`b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6`**
   - Embedded PDB debug path: **`E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb`** — the binary self-identifies its internal project/build as **"knock" v1.1.8**.
   - Imports include `LoadLibraryW/Ex`, `GetProcAddress`, `CreateProcessW` — consistent with a loader/downloader component.
3. **04:13:00 onward** — Immediately after the DLL landed, the host began persistent HTTP beaconing to **72.5.43.29:80** that continued for the rest of the capture (~29 minutes, ~308 requests, GET every ~5–6 seconds with occasional POST). Each request carries a large, largely-static base64-looking blob in the `Cookie` header, uses a fixed non-standard User-Agent, and receives small binary "encrypted-looking" response bodies (most recent attempts get `400 Bad Request`, suggesting the check-in protocol wasn't completing cleanly in this run). No DNS query was made for 72.5.43.29 — the address is hardcoded.

## Malware family
- The downloaded DLL's own PDB string names the project **"knock" (v1.1.8)**. This is a **file-derived artifact, not a public AV/vendor signature match** — no Suricata/IDS alert file was provided in the evidence, and this analysis had no internet access to cross-reference the hash/strings against threat-intel naming.
- **Attribution level: behavioral + embedded-artifact, not signature-confirmed.** The observed chain (bloated obfuscated JS in a fake-invoice ZIP → BITS-fetched DLL "loader" → fixed-IP HTTP beacon with encrypted cookie-carried check-ins) is consistent with a generic loader/bot rather than a well-known, independently-confirmed family name. I am not attaching a public malware-family label (e.g., a named commodity RAT/loader) that this traffic cannot itself prove — doing so would go beyond what's grounded in the pcap.

## Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `72.5.43.29:80/` (HTTP GET/POST beacon, ~308 requests, 04:13:00–04:42:26) — no associated domain, hardcoded IP
- `72.5.43.29:80/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` — payload staging path

**Malicious/lure domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (104.21.55.70) — initial ZIP delivery
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` (172.67.170.159) — callback/tracking URL referenced inside the JS dropper

**Malicious URL**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215`

**Transferred files / hashes**
| File | SHA256 | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Invoice 876597035_003.zip | `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5` | 2,767,804 B | delivered by quote.checkfedexexp.com |
| Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js | `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c` | 6,990,020 B | dropper, inside the ZIP |
| 0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4 (DLL) | `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6` | 159,232 B | fetched via BITS from 72.5.43.29, PDB: `knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb` |

**Note:** other BITS/HTTP transfers in the capture (to `msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com` / Microsoft CDN 199.232.210.172, `acroipm2.adobe.com`, `oneocsp.microsoft.com`) are legitimate Windows/Adobe/OCSP background traffic and are not part of the incident.
